ops.title: The two shapes of a green test that proves nothing
ops.body:
The daemonkit v0.21 migration review of 8df819e..079f313 ran five adversarial rounds and found six tests that ran green while proving nothing. All six fall into two shapes, and the shapes are the useful part, because a reviewer who knows them finds these tests by pattern instead of by luck. A test either asserts the wrong property, which this note calls the converted assertion, or never executes its subject at all, the short-circuit. A green run certifies behavior only after both checks below pass. The sixth instance shows the same shapes apply to the verification steps that vouch for tests, not just to the tests themselves.

## The converted assertion

The test reaches its subject, runs it, and asserts, but the assertion is about the wrong property. Green proves the test's own claim, not the behavior anyone cared about. Three instances surfaced.

The build-skew test at `internal/cli/select_test.go:279#edh6` asserted `strings.Contains(err.Error(), "daemon runtime build is not exact")`, the retired client's wording, where the contract is `errors.Is(err, daemon.ErrDaemonBuildMismatch)`. Under the prose assertion, a message rewrite kills the test while the behavior survives, and a sentinel swap leaves the test green while the fleet's `errors.Is` matches break. Fixed in 7caccc2.

The pre-input disconnect test at `internal/daemon/account_mutation_test.go:468#tdjt` encoded transport disconnect as an explicit `TerminalInputEOF` payload, a leftover from the streaming era when one closed channel expressed both. The unary subject distinguishes them. EOF states that no input is coming and resolves the row; an abandoned start sends nothing and must stay resumable. The test asserted the EOF outcome and passed, certifying the opposite of the disconnect behavior. 22d9934 rebuilt it to drive a real session teardown and assert the row survives unresolved, unstarted, and re-attachable.

The inventory-bracket table in `internal/statusapp/deployment_test.go` carried a refusal arm named "the installed binary held the pid only after the answer", asserting that a PID appearing after the first inventory refuses. It did refuse, but only because any pin failure produces that refusal, not because the appears-after case is correctly refused. It is not. A holder starting mid-observation is a legitimate launchd restart, so the arm pinned wrong behavior with an assertion that held for a reason unrelated to the case it named. 10f3937 recast the arm as a retry; the successor test sits at `internal/statusapp/deployment_test.go:355#bg6k`.

To catch the shape, name the property the test's own name claims, then require the assertion to state that property in contract terms, meaning a sentinel, a typed error, or a state transition, never a rendering of one. Then mutate the subject and require a red run. Swap the sentinel and the skew test must fail, which only the `errors.Is` form does. Collapse the EOF/disconnect distinction and the disconnect test must fail, which only a real-teardown fixture does. Make the bracket accept the appears-after PID and the old refusal arm should have failed; it stayed green, and that gap is the finding. The recurring tells from this review were an assertion on `err.Error()` text, a fixture payload impersonating an input the subject distinguishes, and a table where every arm asserts one coarse refusal.

## The short-circuit

The test never reaches its subject. Some precondition returns early, the code under test never executes, and the test passes because nothing ran.

`TestRepositionAfterTeardownClosesTheReplacement` at `internal/daemon/account_mutation_poll_test.go:287#xp9h` called `pa.reposition(…, 0)` on a wrapper minted at cursor 0. Reposition's first line, the `cursorMatches` guard at `internal/daemon/account_mutation_poll.go:516#kad2`, returns before the teardown-race arm the test exists to prove at `internal/daemon/account_mutation_poll.go:526#x76v` can run. 72f7c31 changed the call at `internal/daemon/account_mutation_poll_test.go:301#tnx7` to reposition to cursor 1, so the call always crosses into the subject.

The review also found a compare-and-swap test whose fixture never produced an actual conflict, so its conflict handling passed without conflicting. That instance is real and its cite is a named gap. The closest commit by name is a23d27b, "mint an owner for the parent-path CAS manager fixture", touching `internal/pool/credential_cas_test.go:464#dh8p`, but the surrounding history reads as red-test maintenance during the migration, not a green test whose subject never ran, and no other commit in the range touches a conflict-asserting CAS test. Do not trust a line number here until someone re-pins it.

To catch the shape, prove the subject was entered instead of trusting that the test returned. The in-tree pattern is the single-flight race test's in-flight gauge at `internal/pool/credential_operation_recovery_test.go:1911#artd`. 5e80c26 added an assertion that at least two retries actually overlapped, turning silent loss of the race into a loud failure, and 24c4787 replaced its scheduling luck with a test-injected settlement gate; round 5 found the gate still scheduler-dependent, so the fully deterministic form is still landing. When the subject is a branch, assert its observable side effect. The reposition fix pairs the closed-refusal error with an attachment-count check, so an early return can no longer satisfy the test. And walk every early return between the test's entry point and its subject holding the fixture's actual values. Cursor 0 against a wrapper minted at cursor 0 is the whole bug.

## The verification step is a test too

The sixth instance was the check meant to vouch for a test. A mutation check, which mutates the subject and requires the test to fail before concluding it has teeth, was itself short-circuited and never reached its own subject, so "we mutation-checked it" was false. No durable record of the specific step survives in the range's commits or notes; the lesson does. A mutation check makes the same claim a test does, that the mutated line ran and the failure came from it, and earns the same scrutiny. Confirm the mutation is in the executed build, confirm the run reached the mutated line, and confirm the failure fires at the assertion naming the subject. A compile error, a skipped suite, or an earlier precondition failure is not teeth. Record which mutation was applied and which assertion caught it; an unrecorded mutation check is a claim, not a check.

## The procedure, in order

1. State the subject, the behavior the test's name claims, in one sentence.
2. Reach. Walk every early return between entry and subject with the fixture's actual values; where reach depends on scheduling, make the test assert reach itself, as the in-flight gauge does.
3. Teeth. Mutate the subject, by inverting the guard, swapping the sentinel, or breaking the distinction, and require a red run whose failure names the subject.
4. Apply steps 2 and 3 to the mutation check itself before repeating anyone's "we verified it".
ops.when: reviewing tests or a test diff, judging whether a suite's green run certifies behavior, writing or auditing a mutation check, or triaging review findings about test coverage
